Somatotroph: Growth hormone and the liver relay
An educational map of adult growth hormone signaling. The geometry, pulse timing and symbols are schematic; they do not represent personal measurements.
A somatotroph in the anterior pituitary releases growth hormone (GH) from granules. GH reaches the nearby capillary in a burst rather than at a steady rate.
Circulating GH reaches the liver and also acts directly on tissues such as skeletal muscle. The fork shows two destinations in the same circulation, not separate vessels from the pituitary.
In response to GH, liver cells make insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) and release it into blood. The liver is a major source of circulating IGF-I. GH and IGF-I are distinct signals.
GH and IGF-I can both act on skeletal muscle and support protein synthesis in adults. The short fiber marks represent that activity, not an increase in muscle size.
Endotext: Growth hormone physiology in adults

A teaching illustration of the adult lactating breast. The shapes, signal symbols and timing are schematic, not measurements of a person or of milk production.
Hypothalamic dopamine normally restrains prolactin release. When that restraint eases, the anterior pituitary lactotroph releases more prolactin (PRL) into blood.
Blood carries PRL to the alveoli
PRL travels in the circulation to the lactating breast. The small sacs at the ends of the duct branches are mammary alveoli, where milk is made.
PRL reaches receptors on the outer, blood-facing side of the secretory cells. The signal does not have to enter the lumen to act.
Secretory cells make milk and release it from their inner surface into the lumen. Oxytocin helps eject milk by contracting cells around the alveolus; that separate action is not shown.
Human ultrasound study: Lactating breast anatomy
Corticotroph: ACTH to the adrenal cortex
A schematic teaching section of the adult pituitary-to-adrenal route. Layers, particle counts and timing do not depict individual anatomy or hormone measurements.
Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) travels from the hypothalamus through pituitary portal vessels. It signals a corticotroph in the anterior lobe to release ACTH.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) enters the general circulation and reaches an adrenal gland above the kidney. The target here is the adrenal cortex, not the kidney.
The moving highlight follows the zona fasciculata, the middle zone of the outer cortex. It is the main source of cortisol. The medulla is the inner region, not the source shown here.
ACTH stimulates cells in the zona fasciculata to make cortisol. Newly made cortisol crosses into nearby blood; cortisol is a different hormone from ACTH.

FSH and LH to the gonads
An educational comparison of the adult ovarian and testicular routes. The sections, signal symbols and intervals do not represent personal hormone levels, cycle timing or fertility.
Hypothalamic nerve terminals release gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) into portal blood. Intermittent pulses signal gonadotrophs in the anterior pituitary.
Gonadotrophs release follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH, circles) and luteinizing hormone (LH, diamonds). Both travel in blood to the gonads. The branches compare ovarian and testicular targets.
Two layers of an ovarian follicle
In a developing follicle, FSH acts on inner granulosa cells and LH acts on outer theca cells. These layers cooperate in making estrogen.
FSH acts on Sertoli cells inside seminiferous tubules to support sperm development. LH acts on Leydig cells between the tubules, stimulating testosterone production.
